prepTasks.word: The idea that has stayed with me

writingModel: The Book That Changed the Way I Read

There are books that you finish and put aside, and there are books that change the way you read everything that comes after. The book that did this for me was Roland Barthes' "Mythologies," a collection of essays that was first published in French in 1957 and that, despite its age, has lost none of its capacity to disturb comfortable assumptions.

Barthes, whose method involves reading cultural objects — advertisements, sports, food — as if they were texts full of hidden meaning, taught me that nothing is innocent. The world that surrounds us is not simply there; it has been constructed and arranged to communicate particular values. Once you have absorbed this idea, which took me several rereads to fully internalise, you cannot look at an advertisement, a news headline, or a public ceremony in the same way.

The essay I found most affecting was "The World of Wrestling," in which Barthes analyses professional wrestling as a kind of theatre whose purpose is not deception but clarity — the opposite of what most people assume. Wrestling, he argues, is a spectacle that makes visible the moral character of its participants in exaggerated form. The wrestlers who villainise themselves do so with full awareness; the audience who responds is not duped but participating.

What Barthes gave me was a way of reading that has remained useful in every field I have since studied. Linguistics, political science, environmental sociology — in each of these, the ideas that surface are embedded in forms that carry assumptions, and those assumptions are worth examining. The moment when I first understood this was also the moment when I stopped reading passively.

The book itself, which is now heavily annotated and whose spine has been cracked in three places, sits on the shelf above my desk. It is the physical object that most visibly represents the change in how I think. Every student who is serious about reading critically should encounter it — or something like it — before the end of their undergraduate degree.

Reading Barthes did not give me answers, which would have been less useful anyway. It gave me a method — one that has proved applicable to everything from news journalism to the language that universities use to describe their own educational mission. The most valuable books are not the ones that tell you what to think, but the ones whose approach to thinking changes your own.

writingTemplate.hint: Use a defining relative clause in your title. "The Book THAT Changed..." ✅
Open with a defining clause contrast. "There are books THAT X, and books THAT Y."

writingTemplate.hint: Introduce your subject with a defining relative clause.

writingTemplate.suffix: . Once you have absorbed this, which ___.
writingTemplate.hint: "The idea THAT..." (defining) + "...which took me time" (sentential which). ✅
